passage: Nursery note, Tuesday. During snack time, Ramesh lined up his grapes and touched each one: "One, two, three, four, five." Jatin had three. Ramesh looked from plate to plate and said, "I got more! Jatin has less." Jatin frowned and counted his own twice, getting three both times. I asked what would make them the same. Ramesh thought for a while, then slid two grapes across. They counted together, and both plates had five. Next week I will add a bead basket to the snack corner. 🙂

qa.q: How many grapes did Jatin have at first?
qa.a: Jatin had three grapes.

qa.q: What was Jatin probably feeling when he frowned and counted his grapes twice?
qa.a: He likely felt it was unfair and wanted to check Ramesh's claim; counting twice shows he was testing whether he really had less.

qa.q: What small step could the teacher try next to keep this counting going?
qa.a: She could give pairs of children beads or blocks to share out and ask, "Who has more? How can we make it the same?"

qa.q: What would change if Ramesh had only glanced at the plates instead of counting one by one?
qa.a: He might have guessed wrongly, and the idea of making the plates equal would not have come from real numbers.

grounding: It shows a child counting objects one by one and comparing which plate has more or less.

passage: At the Sunday haat in their kasba, Nani bought a paper cone of peanuts and tipped some into each child's palm. Sonali, five, counted aloud, pressing each nut with her thumb: "Ek, do, teen, char, paanch, chhe." Her little brother Kishore had a heap too, but kept losing his place after three. "Mine is more," he declared, because his pile looked wider. Sonali laid both piles in two rows on Nani's cloth bag. Her row stretched past his by two nuts. Kishore stared. "Yours is longer," he admitted, and held out his hand. Nani chuckled and gave him two more.

qa.q: Where did Nani buy the peanuts?
qa.a: At the Sunday haat in their kasba.

qa.q: Why did Kishore think his pile was more?
qa.a: He felt confident his pile was more because it looked wider, judging by looks rather than counting, since he kept losing his place after three.

qa.q: How could Nani help Kishore count past three?
qa.a: She could count slowly with him, touching each nut the way Sonali did, or line the nuts in a row so he can keep his place.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Kishore's claim?
qa.a: She seems to find it worth checking rather than arguing about, so she lays the nuts in rows to show the difference plainly.

grounding: It shows a five-year-old counting and using rows to show which pile has more.

passage: On a grey Saturday in Rotterdam, Elif and her neighbour Nour sat on the back step sharing a bag of cherries. Elif made two piles. "Four for you, four for me," she said, counting each red stem. Nour pointed. "Yours has a big one." "Big is not more," Elif said slowly, frowning. "More is the counting." She counted both piles again, her finger bouncing. Four and four. Nour shrugged and swapped one big cherry for a small one anyway, and they both grinned.

qa.q: How many cherries were in each pile?
qa.a: There were four cherries in each pile.

qa.q: What does Elif's slow frown suggest when Nour mentions the big cherry?
qa.a: She seems to be working out the difference between size and number and wants to be sure before she answers.

qa.q: How could an adult nearby build on Elif's idea?
qa.a: They could ask, "Which pile has more cherries, and which pile is heavier?" so she can explore size and number as two different things.

qa.q: How does Nour see fairness differently from Elif?
qa.a: Nour judges by the size of the cherries while Elif judges by the count, so the swap lets both of them feel it is even. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child using counting to decide which amount is more, separate from size.

passage:
"Mumma, this dupatta is a river," Ojas said, spreading it across the floor.
"A river? And what's the steel katori?" Alka asked.
"A boat. No, wait, a helmet for the boat man." He put it on his head.
"And the rolling pin?"
"That's a crocodile. It sleeps under the river."
"Should I be scared?"
"Only if you step in the river, Mumma."
Alka tiptoed around the blue cloth with the laundry basket.
Ojas pointed. "Careful! Your basket is a big ship. It needs a bridge." He laid a slipper across.

qa.q: What did Ojas say the rolling pin was?
qa.a: A crocodile that sleeps under the river.

qa.q: How can you tell Ojas is enjoying inventing new meanings?
qa.a: He changes ideas quickly, even correcting himself with "No, wait," and adds new roles like the bridge without being asked. 😊

qa.q: Which of Alka's choices helped the game grow, and why?
qa.a: She asked open questions and played along by tiptoeing, which invited more ideas instead of correcting him.

qa.q: What would change if Alka had said, "That's just a rolling pin, put it back"?
qa.a: The game would likely stop, and Ojas might learn that his ideas are not welcome at home.

grounding: It shows a child turning everyday household objects into new things in a pretend scenario.

passage: Preschool observation, written by Pradeep, class teacher. Rainy day, no outdoor play, so I gave the group empty cardboard boxes. Zubin climbed into one and announced it was a submarine. Two minutes later it became a post office; he cut a slot with safety scissors and posted leaves as letters. When a friend wanted a car, Zubin said, "It can be both. It drives, then it swims." I asked what else a box could be. He listed a drum, a bed for his toy dog and "a cave for shy people." I will keep the boxes out all week. 😊

qa.q: What did Zubin post through the slot in the box?
qa.a: He posted leaves as letters.

qa.q: What does Zubin's "It can be both" suggest about how he was thinking?
qa.a: He wanted to keep the game going for himself and his friend, and seemed to enjoy combining ideas rather than picking one.

qa.q: What could Pradeep try next to support this kind of play?
qa.a: He could offer more open materials like tubes, cloth and pegs, and keep asking "What else could it be?" without judging the answers.

qa.q: How might the friend who wanted a car feel about Zubin's answer?
qa.a: The friend probably felt included, since their idea was added to the game instead of turned down.

grounding: It shows a child inventing many different uses for a cardboard box during play.

passage: Behind the house, the buffalo dozed while Ankita and her cousin Uday played with whatever lay in the yard. Ankita held up the winnowing tray. "This is a stage. I'm the dancer." Uday offered a dried corn cob. "Microphone!" Then the cob became a rocket, then a pen, then a baby that needed rocking. When Ankita's grandmother wanted the tray back to clean rice, Ankita didn't argue. She turned an empty bucket upside down and drummed on it. "Now we have music instead," she said, and Uday started to dance.

qa.q: What did Uday first say the corn cob was?
qa.a: He said it was a microphone.

qa.q: Why didn't Ankita argue when her grandmother took the tray back?
qa.a: She seemed calm and unbothered, seeing other things in the yard as just as full of possibilities, so losing the tray did not end her game.

qa.q: How could the grandmother gently encourage this play?
qa.a: She could set aside safe spare things like an old pot or a cloth and ask the children what they would turn them into.

qa.q: How might Uday feel playing with Ankita?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy it: his ideas are taken up quickly, so he keeps offering new ones and joins the dance.

grounding: It shows children in a village yard giving farm objects many new pretend uses.

passage: Rain kept the kindergarten indoors, so twenty children played musical statues in a room meant for ten. Pallavi, five, spun with her arms wide, then pulled them in when her elbow brushed Mridul. When the music stopped, she froze on one foot, wobbling, and put a hand on the wall instead of grabbing him. Mridul was hugging everyone who froze near him. A boy squirmed away. Pallavi said, "He doesn't want a hug. Ask first." Mridul let go and froze with his hands on his own knees.

qa.q: What game were the children playing?
qa.a: They were playing musical statues.

qa.q: Why might Pallavi have pulled her arms in after brushing Mridul?
qa.a: She noticed she had touched him and seemed to want to keep out of the other children's space in the crowded room.

qa.q: How could the teacher make the game safer in a crowded room?
qa.a: She could mark a spot for each child with tape or chalk and remind everyone to ask before touching.

qa.q: What was it like for the boy who squirmed away?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable being hugged, and Pallavi's words helped his wish to be noticed without him having to shout.

grounding: It shows a child keeping balance, protecting others' space and speaking up for a peer's body boundary during an active game.

passage: In the colony park in Hyderabad, Lakshmi and Uday were playing hopscotch on squares chalked by the watchman's son. Lakshmi hopped to seven on one foot, arms out like wings, then tipped and landed with both feet down. "Again!" she said. When Uday's turn came he started hopping right behind her. "Wait, I'm too near," Lakshmi said, stepping back so he wouldn't crash into her. Later a girl tugged Lakshmi's plait to tease her. "Don't pull my hair, it hurts," Lakshmi said. The girl let go and said sorry.

qa.q: Which square did Lakshmi reach before she tipped over?
qa.a: She hopped to square seven before she tipped.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi thinking when she said, "Wait, I'm too near"?
qa.a: She seemed to realise they might collide and wanted to give Uday room to hop safely.

qa.q: How could an adult support Lakshmi when someone pulls her hair?
qa.a: Praise her clear words and back her up calmly, while helping the other child practise asking before touching.

qa.q: How did the girl who pulled the plait learn something here?
qa.a: Hearing "it hurts" directly showed her the tease was not fun for Lakshmi, so she stopped and said sorry.

grounding: It shows a child balancing in a hopping game, keeping safe distance and stating her own body boundary.

passage:
"Tickle monster!" Tushar pounced, fingers wiggling.
Nikita shrieked, then went stiff. "Stop. Stop, Tushar."
He froze, hands in the air. "But you were laughing."
"Now I'm not."
Papa looked up from his tea. "What did she say?"
"Stop," Tushar mumbled, shuffling back. "Can I tickle your feet only?"
"No. But we can do the pillow jump."
"Okay! You go first. I'll stand back here so you don't land on me."
Nikita bounced off the sofa cushion, wobbled and caught her balance.
"Wow, you didn't fall!" Tushar cheered.

qa.q: What game did Nikita suggest instead of tickling?
qa.a: She suggested the pillow jump.

qa.q: Why did Tushar say "But you were laughing"?
qa.a: He was confused, because laughing looked like fun to him, and he may have felt a little stung at being stopped.

qa.q: What would you advise Tushar about tickling next time?
qa.a: Ask first, and stop the moment someone says stop, even if they were laughing a second ago.

qa.q: What is it like for Nikita when Tushar freezes at once?
qa.a: She learns her "stop" is respected, which likely makes her happy to keep playing with him.

grounding: It shows siblings honouring a spoken body boundary and giving each other space to balance in active play.

passage:
Monday: Ojas sat on the step tugging at his shoelaces until they knotted. He threw the shoe. Bhavna Didi tied it for him.
Wednesday: He tried again with Didi's "bunny ears" rhyme. One loop flopped. He huffed, then made the loop again.
Saturday: Ojas bent down alone, whispered the rhyme and pulled tight. A bow! He jumped up, shoulders back, chin high, and marched into the kitchen. "Didi, look! I did it myself!" He walked in slow circles so everyone could see his feet.

qa.q: On which day did Ojas tie the bow by himself?
qa.a: He tied it by himself on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Ojas marching in with his chin high suggest?
qa.a: He felt proud of his own effort and wanted everyone to see what he had managed.

qa.q: How could Bhavna respond so his pride stays linked to effort?
qa.a: She could say, "You kept trying all week, and now you can do it!" so he connects the good feeling with practice. 🎉

qa.q: What would change if Bhavna had kept tying his shoes every day?
qa.a: Ojas would have missed the chance to succeed alone, and the proud Saturday moment would not have happened.

grounding: It shows a child standing tall with satisfaction after mastering a skill through his own effort.

passage: The water tanker came late, just as the light was fading, and the whole lane rushed out with buckets. Nirmala had two heavy ones and the baby on her hip. "I can take the small one, Amma," Uday said. He gripped the handle with both hands, walked slowly around the puddles, and set it down by their door without spilling. Nirmala looked in. "Full to the top!" Uday pushed out his chest, pulled his back very straight and went back to wait in the line.

qa.q: Why could Nirmala not carry everything herself?
qa.a: She had two heavy buckets and the baby on her hip.

qa.q: How can you tell Uday felt proud?
qa.a: After she praised the full bucket, he pushed out his chest, straightened his back and went back to the line.

qa.q: What small step could Nirmala take next to build on this?
qa.a: She could give him a small regular job, like carrying the little bucket each time, and notice how carefully he does it.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Uday's help in that rushed moment?
qa.a: To her it was real help at a hard time, not a game, so her praise was likely warm and honest.

grounding: It shows a young child's pride and upright posture after succeeding at a real task under pressure.

passage: Kavitha pressed the crayon so hard it snapped, but the letters stood on the page: K-A-V-I-T-H-A, the V a little crooked. She held the paper up to the window of their flat in Pune so the light came through. Then she carried it to Santosh Mama, who was fixing the fan. "Read it," she said. He read it slowly, like a big announcement. Kavitha's feet did a little dance. She stuck the page on the fridge with a magnet and kept walking past it all afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha stick her page?
qa.a: She stuck it on the fridge with a magnet.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha keep walking past the fridge?
qa.a: She felt proud of writing her own name and seemed to enjoy seeing it again and again.

qa.q: How could Santosh Mama encourage her further?
qa.a: He could ask her to write his name next, or a label for the toolbox, so she gets to use her new skill.

qa.q: Why might Santosh Mama read the name "like a big announcement"?
qa.a: He seemed to understand how big this was for her and wanted to share in her pride.

grounding: It shows a child's satisfaction and delight after writing her name for the first time.

passage: I'm Amandeep. At Biji's birthday, Mummy asked my sister Disha, who is five, to carry the sweets tray to the uncles. She walked very carefully, but near the door the tray tipped and the laddoos rolled everywhere. An aunty said, "Oho, such a big girl and she can't hold a tray." Disha didn't cry. She went under the dining table and put her face on her knees. When I crawled in, she whispered, "I'm a bad girl. I can't do anything." I don't know what else she was thinking, but she stayed there until Biji came.

qa.q: What did the aunty say when the laddoos fell?
qa.a: She said, "Oho, such a big girl and she can't hold a tray."

qa.q: What does Disha hiding and saying "I'm a bad girl" suggest?
qa.a: She seems to feel deeply ashamed of her whole self, not just the spill, after failing at what the grown-ups expected.

qa.q: How could Biji or Mummy help Disha when she comes out?
qa.a: Tell her calmly that spills happen and she is not bad, then let her help pick up the laddoos or try again with a lighter plate.

qa.q: How might the aunty think differently if she had seen Disha under the table?
qa.a: She might realise her words hurt more than the spill did and choose kinder ones.

grounding: It shows a young child concluding she is bad as a person after failing an adult's expectation in public.

passage:
Day one: Miss Varghese gave gold stars to the children who could say the whole poem. Thomas forgot the second line. He was the only one without a star. At home he told Amma, "I'm the stupid one," and wouldn't eat.
Day four: He hid his notebook when his friend Ojas asked to see it.
Day nine: Amma had practised the poem with him as a silly song. In class he said it all. Ojas clapped. Thomas smiled a small smile, but that night he asked, "Am I still stupid?" Amma hugged him. "You never were."

qa.q: What did the teacher give to children who could say the whole poem?
qa.a: She gave them gold stars.

qa.q: What does Thomas calling himself "the stupid one" show?
qa.a: He seems to feel bad about who he is, not just about one forgotten line, because he was the only one without a star.

qa.q: What helped Thomas, and what more could the teacher do?
qa.a: Practising in a playful way helped; the teacher could praise effort and avoid public prizes that leave one child out.

qa.q: How might Ojas see what happened on day nine?
qa.a: He seemed glad for his friend and clapped, probably without knowing how bad Thomas had felt before.

grounding: It shows a child feeling worthless as a person after missing a reward others received, and slowly recovering.

passage: The school van honked twice outside. Ira, four, was still fighting the top button of her uniform, her fingers slipping. "Other children do this in one minute," Zeenat snapped, grabbing the button herself. Ira's arms dropped. She stared at the floor. "I'm a bad Ira. Bad, bad." She didn't pick up her bag. Zeenat stopped. The van honked again. She knelt anyway. "You're not bad. Buttons are hard. Amma was cross because of the van, not you." Ira let out a long breath and reached for her bag.

qa.q: What was Ira trying to do when the van honked?
qa.a: She was trying to fasten the top button of her uniform.

qa.q: Why did Ira say "I'm a bad Ira"?
qa.a: After her mother compared her to other children, she seemed ashamed, as if failing at the button meant she herself was bad.

qa.q: What went right after Zeenat stopped?
qa.a: She knelt, separated the button from Ira's worth and owned her own crossness, which let Ira breathe and move again.

qa.q: What would change on a morning without the van honking?
qa.a: Zeenat might have had time to wait or help calmly, and Ira might never have heard the comparison.

grounding: It shows a small child turning a failed task into a belief that she is bad, and a parent repairing it under time pressure.

passage:
Monday: Baljeet grabbed Tushar's red crayon, and when Tushar tugged back, it snapped. Baljeet dropped both halves and ran to the swings.
Tuesday: He didn't sit next to Tushar at drawing time. He kept looking over, then down at his own paper.
Thursday: Baljeet came to school with a new red crayon in his fist. He held it out. "I broke yours. I pulled it. Sorry." Tushar took it and said, "You can use it first." Baljeet let out a big breath and sat down beside him.

qa.q: What did Baljeet bring to school on Thursday?
qa.a: He brought a new red crayon.

qa.q: What does Baljeet looking over and then down on Tuesday suggest?
qa.a: He seemed to feel bad about breaking the crayon and was avoiding Tushar while still thinking about it.

qa.q: How could a teacher help a child like Baljeet sooner?
qa.a: She could quietly ask what happened and help him say sorry or fix it, so the bad feeling turns into a repair instead of days of avoiding.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt on Thursday?
qa.a: He probably felt respected by the honest apology, which is why he offered to let Baljeet use the crayon first.

grounding: It shows a child recognising the specific wrong he did and showing remorse by apologising and replacing the crayon.

passage: Mangoes were costly that week, so Maa bought just one and kept it on the shelf for Tanvir, who was home with a cough. While Maa was at the tap, Bidisha, six, took a bite. Then another. Soon only half was left. She looked at the sticky seed, and her stomach felt tight. When Tanvir called for his mango, Bidisha went and stood beside Maa. "I ate half of Tanvir's," she said, eyes wet. "I knew it was his." She pushed her own biscuit across to her brother.

qa.q: Why did Maa buy only one mango?
qa.a: Mangoes were costly that week.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's tight stomach suggest?
qa.a: She knew she had done something wrong by eating her brother's mango and felt sorry about it.

qa.q: How could Maa respond in a way that helps Bidisha learn?
qa.a: Thank her for telling the truth, say clearly that eating it was not okay, and let her make it up to Tanvir, as she has started to.

qa.q: What might Tanvir think when Bidisha pushes her biscuit across?
qa.a: He may still be disappointed, but he can see she is sorry and trying to make it up to him. 🙏

grounding: It shows a child admitting a specific wrong and feeling remorse, with scarce money making it matter more.

passage: In the sandpit behind their building in Kochi, Dilnaz had built a tall castle with a shell on top. Jomon, who had just lost the race to the gate, kicked it flat. Dilnaz's mouth opened, but no sound came out. Jomon looked at the lumpy sand and then at her face. His ears went red. He sat down and began patting the sand back into a pile with both hands. "I kicked it," he mumbled. "That was mean. I'll make it again." He placed the shell on top, crooked.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz put on top of her castle?
qa.a: She put a shell on top.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when his ears went red?
qa.a: He seemed to feel guilty, realising that kicking her castle was a mean thing he had done.

qa.q: What would you advise Jomon for the next time he loses a race?
qa.a: Notice the angry feeling and take a breath or stomp somewhere away from other people's things before acting.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilnaz to see Jomon rebuilding?
qa.a: Her shock may ease, since he names what he did and tries to fix it, even though the castle is not quite the same.

grounding: It shows a child recognising his own specific wrong action and feeling remorse strong enough to repair it.

passage: The wedding hall was loud with drums when someone's uncle lifted Lakshmi onto a chair. "Dance for us, little one!" Fifty faces turned. Phone cameras rose. Lakshmi, five, had danced all morning with her cousin Pema behind the curtain, but now her hands went to her face. She peeked through her fingers and tucked her chin. The uncle clapped louder. Pema climbed up beside her, took her hand and wiggled her own shoulders. Lakshmi giggled into Pema's sleeve, then slid down and hid behind her mother's sari.

qa.q: Who lifted Lakshmi onto a chair?
qa.a: Someone's uncle lifted her onto a chair.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi cover her face when the faces turned to her?
qa.a: The sudden attention felt like too much, and she became shy and self-conscious even though she had enjoyed dancing in private.

qa.q: How could the adults have handled it better?
qa.a: Ask her first, or let her dance with Pema among other children, instead of putting her alone on a chair in front of cameras.

qa.q: How did Pema see the moment?
qa.a: She seemed to notice Lakshmi's discomfort and joined her so she would not be alone in the spotlight.

grounding: It shows a child's sudden shyness when a crowd's unwanted attention lands on her.

passage: At her sixth birthday in the society clubhouse, the lights went off and everyone started singing. Shalini had been racing around with Binita all evening. Now twenty grown-ups and children stood in a ring around her, every face looking her way. The candles glowed. Shalini's cheeks went hot. She pulled her frock over her knees, ducked her head below the table edge and whispered, "Stop singing." Binita crouched beside her. "Blow fast and it finishes," she whispered back. Shalini blew, then hid her face in Binita's shoulder, grinning.

qa.q: Where was Shalini's sixth birthday party held?
qa.a: In the society clubhouse.

qa.q: What does Shalini ducking and whispering "Stop singing" suggest?
qa.a: She felt suddenly shy and flustered with everyone looking at her, even though she was happy about her party.

qa.q: What could Shalini's family try at the next party?
qa.a: Let her blow the candles with a friend beside her, or keep the circle smaller, so the attention feels lighter.

qa.q: Why might Binita understand what Shalini needed?
qa.a: As another child she may know that feeling, and she offered a simple way to make it end quickly. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child's hot cheeks and hiding when a whole room's attention suddenly turns on her.

passage:
"Hemant, come, say your rhyme for Chachi!" Nani called.
"No."
"Arre, you said it so nicely to me yesterday."
"Not now." Hemant wrapped himself in the curtain.
Chachi laughed. "Look, he's shy! So cute!"
"I'm not cute," came a muffled voice.
His cousin Dilnaz peeked in. "Want to say it just to me, in here?"
A pause. "Twinkle, twinkle..." he whispered.
"Nice," Dilnaz whispered back. "Nobody else heard."
A minute later Hemant came out, cheeks pink, and went straight to the biscuits.

qa.q: Where did Hemant hide?
qa.a: He wrapped himself in the curtain.

qa.q: Why did Hemant say "I'm not cute"?
qa.a: Being laughed at and called cute in front of everyone made him feel more embarrassed, and he wanted the attention to stop.

qa.q: How could Nani ask differently next time?
qa.a: She could ask quietly first, or let him say it to one person, as Dilnaz did, instead of calling him out in front of guests.

qa.q: What would change if Chachi had just smiled and carried on talking?
qa.a: Hemant might have felt less watched and come out sooner, maybe even saying the rhyme.

grounding: It shows a child hiding from overwhelming adult attention and recovering once the audience shrinks.

passage: Thunder cracked, and everyone in the lane ran for cover. Salma, five, stood under the tin roof of the tea stall with her father. Across the road, Asif was crying, holding a kite that had turned into wet paper. Salma's face crumpled too. She tugged Abbu's kurta. "Asif's kite is dead." When the rain eased, she walked over, holding her father's hand, and stood close to Asif without saying anything. Then she patted his arm twice. "Poor kite," she said softly.

qa.q: Where did Salma wait out the rain?
qa.a: Under the tin roof of the tea stall with her father.

qa.q: What does Salma's face crumpling suggest?
qa.a: She felt sad along with Asif when she saw him crying over his ruined kite.

qa.q: How could Abbu build on Salma's feeling?
qa.a: He could name it, like "You feel sad for Asif," and ask what might help, such as making a paper kite together once it is dry. ❤️

qa.q: How might Asif feel with Salma standing close and patting his arm?
qa.a: He may feel less alone in his upset, even though the kite is still ruined.

grounding: It shows a young child feeling sorrow when she sees another child's distress in a storm.

passage: Outside the Kolkata market, a scooter clipped Lalit Kaka's cart, and his tomatoes rolled into the gutter. The old man sat on the kerb and rubbed his forehead. Pooja, six, stopped licking her ice lolly. She watched him pick up one squashed tomato, then another. "Ma, he looks so sad," she said, and her own lip shook. On the walk home she kept turning back to look. At dinner she pushed her rice around the plate. "Will Lalit Kaka have money for food?" she asked.

qa.q: What happened to Lalit Kaka's tomatoes?
qa.a: A scooter clipped his cart and the tomatoes rolled into the gutter.

qa.q: Why did Pooja push her rice around at dinner?
qa.a: She was still sad and worried for Lalit Kaka and could not stop thinking about him.

qa.q: How could Ma answer Pooja's question gently?
qa.a: Admit she does not know, and suggest they buy vegetables from him next time, which gives Pooja a small way to act.

qa.q: What might Lalit Kaka be dealing with that Pooja only partly sees?
qa.a: He has lost his goods and a day's earnings, while Pooja sees mostly his sad face and the squashed tomatoes.

grounding: It shows a child's lingering sorrow and concern after seeing an old man's distress.

passage:
"Mumma, why are your eyes wet?"
"Oh, it's nothing, Deepu. Onions."
"You're not cutting onions." Deepika climbed onto the stool. "Your face is sad."
Sudha sighed. "My friend Rekha moved far away today. I'll miss her."
Deepika's chin wobbled. "Like when Mitthu flew away?"
"A bit like that."
"I was sad for a long time." She leaned against Sudha's arm. "Now I'm sad for you too."
"Thank you, beta."
"Can we draw Rekha Aunty a picture?"

qa.q: What reason did Sudha give first for her wet eyes?
qa.a: She said it was onions.

qa.q: How can you tell Deepika felt sorrow for her mother?
qa.a: Her chin wobbled, she leaned against Sudha's arm and said, "Now I'm sad for you too."

qa.q: How could Sudha respond to Deepika's idea?
qa.a: Say yes and draw together, which shows Deepika that a caring feeling can become a kind action. 🤍

qa.q: What would change if Sudha had kept insisting it was onions?
qa.a: Deepika might feel confused that her reading of the sad face was wrong, and they would miss sharing the feeling.

grounding: It shows a child noticing a parent's sadness and feeling sorrow on her behalf.

passage: On the school picnic, Miss was busy counting heads by the bus, and the field was noisy with forty children. Gautam tripped on a root and sat holding his knee, lips pressed tight. Nobody else noticed. Zubin did. He ran over and squatted down. "Does it hurt?" Gautam nodded. Zubin blew on the scrape the way his mother did, then took off his cap and fanned it. "I'll get Miss," he said, and ran off shouting, "Miss! Gautam is hurt!"

qa.q: What was Miss doing when Gautam fell?
qa.a: She was counting heads by the bus.

qa.q: Why did Zubin blow on the scrape?
qa.a: He wanted to make Gautam's pain better and copied what his mother does to comfort him.

qa.q: How could Miss respond to Zubin afterwards?
qa.a: Thank him for noticing and fetching help, so he knows that telling an adult is part of caring.

qa.q: What is it like for Gautam when Zubin squats beside him?
qa.a: He is no longer alone with the pain in a busy, noisy field; someone has seen him.

grounding: It shows a child noticing a peer's pain in a busy place and trying simple comfort before getting help.

passage: Jasleen came home from her office in Chandigarh, lay on the sofa and pressed her fingers to her forehead. The TV stayed off. Sonali, four, stopped building her tower. She stared at her mother's closed eyes, then fetched her own small pillow and pushed it under Jasleen's head. Next she brought her soft rabbit and tucked it under Mumma's arm. "Rabbit makes it better," she whispered, and patted Jasleen's hair very lightly, as if touching a bubble.

qa.q: What did Sonali tuck under her mother's arm?
qa.a: She tucked her soft rabbit under Mumma's arm.

qa.q: What was Sonali probably thinking when she stared at her mother's closed eyes?
qa.a: She seemed to sense that Mumma was hurting and wanted to make her feel better.

qa.q: How could Jasleen show Sonali that her comfort mattered?
qa.a: She could open her eyes for a moment and say, "Thank you, that helps," so Sonali learns her caring works. 🤍

qa.q: If you were Jasleen, what would you want in that moment?
qa.a: Probably quiet and gentle care, which is just what Sonali's whisper and light touch offered.

grounding: It shows a small child noticing her mother's pain and offering her own comfort objects.

passage:
"Ow!" Ishita shook her hand. A thin red line showed on her finger.
Rukmini dropped her scissors. "You're bleeding!"
"It stings." Ishita's eyes filled.
"Wait, wait." Rukmini ran to her schoolbag and came back with a cartoon plaster. "Paati keeps this for me."
"I can't open it."
"I can." Rukmini peeled it and stuck it on, crooked. "Now kiss it better." She kissed the air above the plaster.
Ishita sniffed. "It still stings a bit."
"Then hold my hand till it stops."

qa.q: Where did Rukmini get the plaster from?
qa.a: From her schoolbag, where Paati keeps it for her.

qa.q: What might Rukmini have been worried about when she dropped her scissors?
qa.a: She was alarmed to see Ishita bleeding and wanted to help her straight away.

qa.q: How could a teacher support this moment?
qa.a: Check the cut, thank Rukmini for her kind help, and explain that telling an adult about a cut is a good step too.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Rukmini's offer to hold hands?
qa.a: Even though it still stings, she likely feels comforted knowing her friend will stay with her.

grounding: It shows a child noticing a friend's pain and trying simple comfort such as a plaster, a kiss and hand-holding.

passage: On the balcony of their flat in Mumbai, Farida landed on the longest snake and slid all the way from 98 to 7. Uma rolled a six and won. Farida's face went red. She swept the counters off the board. "Not fair!" She stomped to the corner and sat with her arms crossed, breathing loudly through her nose. Uma waited. After a while Farida's shoulders came down. She picked up a counter from the floor and brought it back. "One more game," she said. "I'm green this time."

qa.q: Which square did Farida slide down from?
qa.a: She slid from 98 all the way to 7.

qa.q: What does Farida's loud breathing, followed by her shoulders coming down, show?
qa.a: She was angry and disappointed, but she calmed herself in the corner instead of staying upset.

qa.q: How could an adult help Farida the next time she loses?
qa.a: Name the feeling, like "That snake felt so unfair!", let her take a short break, then welcome her back without a lecture.

qa.q: What was it like for Uma to wait?
qa.a: She may have been startled when the counters flew, but her patience gave Farida room to recover and play again.

grounding: It shows a child's brief angry outburst after losing a game and her own recovery within minutes.

passage:
"My tower! It fell!" Arohi kicked a block.
"Oh no," said Mehak. "It was so tall."
"I hate blocks! I'm never playing again!" Arohi flopped onto the rug, face down.
Mehak sat beside her and said nothing for a bit. Then: "Want to count to five with me?"
"No." A pause. "One, two..." muffled into the rug.
"Three, four, five."
Arohi rolled over, eyes wet. "It had a flag on top."
"We can make a flag again. Want the wide blocks at the bottom this time?"
Arohi sat up and grabbed a wide one.

qa.q: What did Arohi say had been on top of her tower?
qa.a: She said it had a flag on top.

qa.q: Why did Arohi say "I hate blocks"?
qa.a: She was upset and disappointed that her tall tower fell, and the words came out of that frustration. 😢

qa.q: Which of Mehak's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting quietly and offering to count gave Arohi time to calm down without being told off, and the wide-block idea gave her a way back.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when Arohi flopped face down?
qa.a: She may have felt a bit helpless at first, but she stayed calm, which kept the upset small.

grounding: It shows a child recovering from a small disappointment within minutes, helped by counting and a new plan.

passage: Teacher's note, KG-B, written by Indu. Musical chairs today. Elizabeth was out in the second round. Last month this would have meant a long cry under the table. Today she stamped once, said "Aww!" loudly, and her lip trembled. Then she took three big breaths, the way we practised with "balloon belly," and went to sit on the cheering bench. By the fourth round she was clapping for her friends. I told her I saw her breathing. She grinned. I will share the balloon breath with her parents. 👍

qa.q: How many big breaths did Elizabeth take?
qa.a: She took three big breaths.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's trembling lip followed by clapping suggest?
qa.a: She felt disappointed about being out, but managed the feeling and even began enjoying her friends' game.

qa.q: Why is Indu's plan to share the balloon breath with the parents useful?
qa.a: Elizabeth can use the same calming trick at home, so the skill gets practised in more places.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's friends experience the change?
qa.a: Instead of a long upset, they get her cheers from the bench, which makes the game happier for everyone.

grounding: It shows a child bouncing back from losing a game with a practised calming breath rather than a long meltdown.
